analysis.one_liner: Phases lead out of paint, toys, packaging, and batteries, and requires recycling of used lead-acid batteries.
analysis.headline: The bill cleared a House subcommittee by voice vote on August 11, 1994, but with no cosponsors it was never taken up by the full committee or voted on by either chamber before the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Toxic Substances Control Act to cut lead out of everyday products: paint above 0.06 percent lead, toys and game pieces above 0.1 percent, curtain weights, newspaper and magazine inks, glass coatings, and packaging with intentionally added lead. It would ban throwing lead-acid batteries into landfills or incinerators and instead require retailers to take them back, charge a $10 deposit on new car batteries without a trade-in, and post recycling notices. It would also phase out mercury in common household batteries, require labels warning that batteries must be recycled, and direct EPA to inventory lead-containing products and label risky ones.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and adults exposed to lead. The bill's own findings call lead poisoning the most prevalent environmental disease among American children, with children under 7 at special risk of permanent neurologic damage [S3]. Households would also benefit from cleaner recycling of car batteries and fewer lead and mercury batteries in the trash. The fishing-sinker provision would benefit small tackle makers and the up to 1.6 million anglers who make their own sinkers, by urging EPA to favor labeling and education over a nationwide ban [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Bans processing (after 1 year) and sale (after 2 years) of paint with more than 0.06 percent lead, toys and game pieces above 0.1 percent, residential curtain weights, and leaded newspaper and magazine inks, with glass coatings phased in over 5 to 6 years [S3].

Prohibits landfilling or incinerating lead-acid batteries and requires them to be delivered to retailers, recyclers, smelters, or collection programs, with retailers accepting used batteries and charging a refundable $10 deposit when no trade-in is returned [S3].

Phases out intentionally added mercury in alkaline-manganese, zinc-carbon, and mercuric-oxide batteries between 1995 and 1997, and requires removable, labeled rechargeable batteries so they can be recycled rather than discarded [S3].

Directs EPA to survey and inventory all lead-containing products in commerce, list and label those posing unreasonable health or environmental risks, and appoint a Coordinator for Lead Activities; authorizes $25 million for fiscal 1995 and roughly $70 million more over three years [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers of lead-containing paint, toys, inks, glass coatings, and packaging would bear reformulation costs, and packaging distributors would face tightening limits down to 100 parts per million within seven years. Battery manufacturers, wholesalers, and retailers would bear take-back, labeling, posting, and deposit costs, with penalties up to $10,000 per violation [S3]. Some costs would likely reach consumers through prices.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall heavily on battery retailers and manufacturers, including mandatory take-back and a $10 deposit, and reformulation of paint, inks, and packaging; some of these costs would likely be passed to consumers through higher prices [S3].

Some transitions are slow: the bill exempts several industrial and vehicle paints pending EPA determinations that substitutes exist, and if no substitute is found, processing restrictions for those uses would not begin until 13 to 14 years after enactment [S3].

A sense-of-Congress provision urges EPA not to finalize a nationwide ban on lead, brass, or zinc fishing sinkers, citing waterbird poisoning that EPA itself could not quantify, while noting substitutes can cost eight to ten times as much and a ban would affect up to 1.6 million anglers who make their own sinkers [S3].
The battery provisions would preempt state and local removability and environmental labeling rules that are not identical, limiting states that wanted stricter requirements [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health upside is large and the bill's own findings describe lead as causing permanent neurologic harm to children, while the main costs are reformulation and recycling logistics that many industries had already begun to absorb as lead uses declined. The slowest phase-outs and the fishing-sinker carve-out show real compromises with affected industries, but the core restrictions are straightforward and address a proven toxin rather than a debatable one.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee on August 1, 1994, and a subcommittee approved an amended version by voice vote ten days later, but the full committee never reported it and no chamber ever voted on it before the Congress ended in January 1995 [S5].

narrative.text: Representative Al Swift introduced the bill on August 1, 1994, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce; he had no cosponsors [S1][S4][S5].
On August 11, 1994, the Subcommittee on Transportation and Hazardous Materials held a markup and forwarded an amended version to the full committee by voice vote [S5].
No further action was taken: the full committee never reported the bill, no floor vote occurred in either chamber, and the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995, killing the bill [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Manufacturers of lead-containing paint, toys, packaging, and batteries avoided the reformulation and take-back costs the bill would have imposed, while children and communities exposed to lead gained nothing. Anglers and small tackle makers also kept a lead-sinker ban off the books through the bill's own provision, but only on paper since the bill never passed.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no cosponsors, so the record shows only a single Democratic sponsor and a subcommittee voice vote; the partisan shape of the fight cannot be determined from the record.

industries.industry: Battery manufacturers, retailers, and lead smelters
industries.note: The bill imposes real costs: take-back duties, a $10 refundable deposit, warning labels, point-of-sale notices, and penalties up to $10,000 per violation. At the same time, it locks in a mandatory recycling channel that routes every used lead-acid battery through retailers, wholesalers, and regulated smelters, guaranteeing them the collection and recycling business [S3].

Restrictions on processing and selling paint above 0.06 percent lead would force reformulation or exit, though industrial, vehicle, and lead-chromate uses get multi-year exemption windows pending EPA findings on substitutes [S3].

Packaging with intentionally added lead would be barred after four years, incidental lead capped at 100 parts per million within seven years, and leaded newspaper and magazine inks prohibited; distributors must keep signed certificates of compliance [S3].

industries.industry: Fishing tackle manufacturers and home lure makers
industries.note: The bill's sense-of-Congress section urges EPA not to finalize its proposed nationwide ban on lead, brass, or zinc sinkers, protecting small manufacturers who cannot afford to retool and the 1.6 million anglers who make their own sinkers, but leaving the waterbird lead-poisoning risk EPA identified unaddressed [S3].
